key_insight: Robotic MAG welding of 10-mm S355MC steel showed much more consistent qualification outcomes and impact-energy dispersion than manual welding, with a physics-informed surrogate capturing representative stress–strain behavior within the tested records.
engineering_relevance: The results suggest robotic welding can deliver higher process robustness and more predictable mechanical properties for structural steel fabrication, but the findings are campaign-specific and not yet validated across independent weldments.
method: EN ISO 15614-1 qualification tests compared robotic vs manual MAG welds on S355MC steel.
Destructive specimen testing supported sample-based capability estimates, including rule-of-three upper bounds and exploratory C pL values.
A general regression neural network reconstructed representative stress–strain curves and assessed within-record prediction error.
evidence_signal: Among 36 robotic specimens no non-conforming outcome was observed, while 5 of 18 manual specimens were non-conforming; Charpy standard deviation was 4.6–5.1 J for robotic modes versus 19.5 J for manual welding, and surrogate RMSEs were 0.37–0.48 MPa.
watch_item: The statistics come from one qualification campaign and single weldment sources, so process-level generalization and transfer to new weldments remain untested.
paper_title: Experimental qualification and physics-informed predictive modelling of robotic and manual MAG welding of S355MC steel
